section.title: The Shepherds of Israel
section.sectionRationale: This chapter is the summit of Ezekiel's turn from judgment to restoration: after Israel's failed shepherds are indicted for feeding themselves instead of the flock, the LORD Himself promises to search for His scattered sheep, and then sets over them 'My servant David', one shepherd who fulfils what every human shepherd could not.
section.thesis: Because Israel's own shepherds fed themselves and scattered the flock, the LORD Himself becomes their Shepherd, seeking the lost and binding up the injured, and appoints His servant David as the one shepherd who will feed them under a covenant of peace, a promise fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the woeful indictment of Israel's self-serving shepherds; the LORD's own promise to search for, gather, and tend His flock; His just judgment between the fat sheep and the lean; and the appointment of one shepherd, His servant David, under an everlasting covenant of peace.

units.label: Woe to Israel's shepherds
units.note: leaders who fed themselves instead of the flock

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“Son of man, prophesy against the {{roeh|shepherds}} of Israel. Prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?
You eat the fat, wear the wool, and butcher the fattened sheep, but you do not feed the flock.
You have not strengthened the weak, healed the sick, bound up the injured, brought back the strays, or searched for the lost. Instead, you have ruled them with violence and cruelty.
They were scattered for lack of a shepherd, and when they were scattered they became food for all the wild beasts.
My flock went astray on all the mountains and every high hill. They were scattered over the face of all the earth, with no one to search for them or seek them out.’

units.label: I Myself will search for My flock

verses.text: Therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD:

‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, because My flock lacks a shepherd and has become prey and food for every wild beast, and because My shepherds did not search for My flock but fed themselves instead,
therefore, you shepherds, hear the word of the LORD!’

This is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will demand from them My flock and remove them from tending the flock, so that they can no longer feed themselves. For I will deliver My flock from their mouths, and it will no longer be food for them.’
For this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.

As a shepherd looks for his scattered sheep when he is among the flock, so I will look for My flock. 
I will rescue them from all the places to which they were scattered on a day of clouds and darkness.

I will bring them out from the peoples, gather them from the countries, and bring them into their own land. I will feed them on the mountains of Israel, in the ravines, and in all the settlements of the land.

I will feed them in good pasture, and the lofty mountains of Israel will be their grazing land. There they will lie down in a good grazing land; they will feed in rich pasture on the mountains of Israel.
I will tend My flock and make them lie down, declares the Lord GOD.
I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak; but the sleek and strong I will destroy. I will shepherd them with justice.’

units.label: Judgment between sheep and sheep
units.note: the fat, pushy sheep and the lean, trampled ones

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says to you, My flock: ‘I will judge between one sheep and another, between the rams and the goats.

Is it not enough for you to feed on the good pasture? Must you also trample the rest of the pasture with your feet? Is it not enough for you to drink the clear waters? Must you also muddy the rest with your feet?
Why must My flock feed on what your feet have trampled, and drink what your feet have muddied?’
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says to them: ‘Behold, I Myself will judge between the fat sheep and the lean sheep.
Since you shove with flank and shoulder, butting all the weak ones with your horns until you have scattered them abroad,
I will save My flock, and they will no longer be prey. I will judge between one sheep and another.

units.label: One shepherd, My servant David
units.note: the appointed shepherd and the covenant of peace

verses.text: I will appoint over them one shepherd, My {{eved_david|servant David}}, and he will feed them. He will feed them and be their shepherd.
I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them. I, the LORD, have spoken.
I will make with them a {{berit_shalom|covenant of peace}} and rid the land of wild animals, so that they may dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the forest.
I will make them and the places around My hill a blessing. I will send down showers in season, showers of blessing.

The trees of the field will give their fruit, and the land will yield its produce; My flock will be secure in their land. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke and delivered them from the hands that enslaved them.
They will no longer be prey for the nations, and the beasts of the earth will not consume them. They will dwell securely, and no one will frighten them.
And I will raise up for them a garden of renown, and they will no longer be victims of famine in the land or bear the scorn of the nations.
Then they will know that I, the LORD their God, am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are My people,’ declares the Lord GOD.
‘You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God,’ declares the Lord GOD.”

roeh.gloss: Shepherd, a common ancient Near Eastern title for a king's duty to protect and provide for his people. Israel's kings, priests, and civic leaders are indicted under this title for feeding themselves instead of the flock.

eved_david.gloss: 'My servant David.' Since David had already died centuries before Ezekiel, this is a prophetic title for the coming heir of David's throne, the Messiah, who finally does what David and every other shepherd-king could not.

berit_shalom.gloss: Covenant of peace, a single, comprehensive covenant binding together security, provision, and right relationship with God into one lasting promise, echoed again in Ezekiel 37:26.

basic.context: Israel's leaders, the 'shepherds', have fed themselves at the flock's expense: eating the fat, wearing the wool, ruling with force, never healing the sick or seeking the lost. So the sheep scattered and became prey. In response, God does something this whole book has been building toward: He says, 'I Myself will search for My flock,' and then appoints 'My servant David' as the one shepherd who will tend them under an everlasting covenant of peace.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real judgment on Israel's actual historical kings, priests, and civic leaders, using shepherd imagery that was a standard ancient Near Eastern description of a king's duty. Its christological weight is not read into the text; the New Testament itself identifies Jesus as the fulfillment of the promised shepherd, most explicitly in John 10.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel's failed leaders are ro'im, shepherds, a common royal title for a king's duty to protect and provide. Against their failure, God promises one shepherd, His eved David, servant David, and a berit shalom, covenant of peace, binding promises of security and blessing into a single lasting bond.
basic.typology: David had been dead for centuries by Ezekiel's day, so 'My servant David' points beyond the historical king to a coming heir of David's line who will finally do what David and every other shepherd-king could not. Jesus says directly, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and 'there shall be one flock and one shepherd,' John 10:16, echoing Ezekiel 34:23-24 precisely.
basic.christ: Jesus explicitly claims the identity this chapter promises. Where Israel's shepherds fed themselves and scattered the flock, Jesus feeds His sheep and lays down His life for them, John 10:11-15. Where God said, 'I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out' (v11), Jesus tells the parable of the lost sheep and says the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 15:4-7, 19:10. He is both the LORD who Himself shepherds His flock and the appointed servant-shepherd descended from David, uniting deity and Davidic humanity in one Person.
basic.god: God is a jealous Shepherd, personally offended when His sheep are fed on by those He entrusted with their care; He judges the false shepherds directly, 'Behold, I am against the shepherds' (v10), and He judges even within the flock, between the fat, pushy sheep and the lean, trampled ones (vv17-22). Yet His anger at bad shepherding flows from tender, personal love: He searches, gathers, binds up, strengthens, and finally shepherds them Himself.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:11-16 shows Jesus claiming the title and role this chapter promises directly. Luke 15:4-7 dramatizes God's promise to seek the lost sheep Himself. 1 Peter 2:25 applies this chapter's language directly to Christ as Shepherd and Overseer of souls. Revelation 7:17 shows the Lamb Himself becoming the flock's Shepherd forever.
basic.oneStory: This is the summit of the turn toward restoration: failed human shepherds are judged, and God Himself steps in to seek, gather, and tend His scattered flock, appointing His servant David as the one shepherd under an everlasting covenant of peace. Every page after this runs toward the Good Shepherd, Jesus Christ, who lays down His life for the sheep and gathers one flock under Himself forever.

context.literary:
Chapter 34 is the first chapter of the book's new half to speak in the voice of restoration, and it sits directly after the news of Jerusalem's fall in 33:21. It is built in four movements, each introduced by a fresh word-event formula or a 'therefore'. Verses 1 to 6 are an indictment, which begins with a woe and a question. Verses 7 to 16 are the sentence on the shepherds and the promise that God will act Himself. Verses 17 to 22 turn on the flock, now sorted into fat and lean, strong and weak. Verses 23 to 31 give the settlement: one shepherd, a covenant of peace, a land at rest, and a declaration of belonging.

The chapter plays on a single metaphor and never lets it go. Because the verb for shepherding and feeding is the same, the accusation 'who only feed themselves' in verse 2 is also a statement of failed shepherding. The catalogue of verse 4 is a list of five duties, strengthening, healing, binding, bringing back and searching, and verse 16 picks up the same list and reverses it, so that what the shepherds did not do, God will do. That mirror is the chapter's central structure. The sins are named once, and the remedy is spelled out in the same terms.

Another pattern is the repeated 'I Myself'. The first person singular is heavy in verses 11 to 31: 'I will search', 'I will rescue', 'I will feed', 'I will judge'. The shift from the shepherds' failure to God's own action is signalled in the Hebrew by the pronoun, so the reader is meant to feel the contrast between 'you' in verses 2 to 10 and 'I' in verses 11 to 16.

The chapter ends with the covenant formula that runs through the whole book, 'You are My flock... and I am your God', verse 31. It begins in judgment on kings and ends in belonging, and it is therefore a small model of the pattern of the book's second half.
context.historical:
Shepherd was a standard royal title across the ancient Near East. Kings in Mesopotamia and Egypt were praised as shepherds of their people, and the duty of the title was protection, provision and justice. Israel inherited the idiom and had a ready example in David, who was called from the sheepfold to shepherd God's people, 2 Samuel 7:8 and Psalm 78:70-72. When Ezekiel preached, he addressed the last kings of Judah and the officials of their courts, who had taxed, taken and judged for their own advantage. Jeremiah's parallel condemnation, Jeremiah 23:1-4, was made in the same years, and Ezekiel's own earlier charges against the princes of Israel appear in 19:1-9 and 22:25-29.

The immediate setting is the exile after Jerusalem's fall, 33:21. The flock has literally been scattered. Some are in Babylon, some in Egypt, some in neighbouring lands, and some are left among the ruins of Judah. The 'wild beasts' of verses 5, 8 and 25 are both real animals that moved into the empty countryside and the nations that preyed on a weak people. The language also looks back to the covenant curses and blessings of Leviticus 26, where wild beasts are loosed on a disobedient land, 26:22, and removed from an obedient one, 26:6.

The sorting in verses 17 to 22 reflects the realities of a flock in a drought. The strong animals muddy the water and trample the grazing, leaving the weak to drink what is left. Ezekiel is describing social injustice inside Israel, the rich and powerful among the people who exploited their poorer neighbours, a theme he and other prophets raised often, Isaiah 5:8 and Amos 2:6-7.

The promise of 'My servant David' was spoken about four centuries after the historical David. The throne had just been destroyed, and Jehoiachin was held in Babylon. The first hearers would have understood a promise that the line would be restored.
context.canonical:
The shepherd image runs from the beginning of the Bible to its last chapters. Jacob speaks of 'the God who has been my shepherd all my life', Genesis 48:15, and Psalm 23:1 begins with 'The LORD is my shepherd'. Psalm 80:1 calls Him the Shepherd of Israel, and Psalm 100:3, with Psalm 95:7, names the people as the sheep of His pasture, which verse 31 of this chapter echoes. Moses asks that the congregation not be 'like sheep without a shepherd', Numbers 27:17, and the long history of Israel's kings measured every ruler by that standard.

Ezekiel's chapter is the high point of the prophetic critique. Jeremiah 23:1-4 and 3:15 promise good shepherds, Zechariah 11 returns to the theme with three shepherds and a worthless one, and Isaiah 56:9-12 describes leaders who are 'shepherds with no discernment'. Isaiah 40:11 is the tender counterpart, 'He tends His flock like a shepherd', and Micah 5:4 promises a ruler who will 'stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD'. Ezekiel 37:24 returns to this chapter, saying 'there will be one shepherd for all of them'.

The New Testament places Jesus at the centre of this promise. Matthew 9:36 says He had compassion on crowds 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd', and Matthew 18:12-14 and Luke 15:4-7 turn Ezekiel's 'I will seek the lost' into parables. In John 10 He says, 'I am the good shepherd', verse 11, and speaks of one flock and one shepherd, verse 16. The same title recurs in Hebrews 13:20, 1 Peter 2:25 and 5:2-4, where the Chief Shepherd stands behind every human elder, and in Revelation 7:17, where the Lamb in the centre of the throne 'will be their shepherd'. Paul tells the elders of Ephesus to be shepherds of the church of God, Acts 20:28.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel is told to prophesy against the shepherds, but he is speaking to the whole house of Israel in exile, and he has two aims. The first is to explain why the flock is scattered. It would have been easy for the exiles to conclude that God had failed or that He was weaker than Babylon's gods. Chapter 34 gives the real cause, that the people placed in charge of them used the office for themselves. It tells the exiles that their situation is no sign of the LORD's neglect. It is the result of the neglect of those He appointed.

The second aim is to give the scattered flock a reason to hope that does not depend on the quality of future human leaders. The point is that when the earthly structures have failed, God will not simply appoint better managers. He will come Himself, and He will raise up a servant from David's house who truly shepherds. The prophecy is meant to make its hearers long for that and wait for it.

There is also a pastoral warning inside the promise. The sorting in verses 17 to 22 tells the sheep that they are not simply victims. Some of them are the cause of other sheep's suffering, and God will judge between them. Any hearer who thought of himself as a sheep and not a shepherd needed to hear that he could also be a trampler.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes the failure of Israel's leaders and God's response, and it promises a future. It does not hand every reader the title of shepherd or give a list of commands to be followed by any leader on his own. The promises of verses 11 to 16 and 23 to 31 are statements about what God Himself will do, and no human shepherd can do them. A pastor who reads 'I will seek the lost' as his own programme is claiming a task that belongs to the Lord, and at best he is serving under Him.

What does carry over is the standard. The catalogue of verse 4 is the measure of faithful leadership in the church. 1 Peter 5:2-4 echoes it directly, telling elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, 'not lording it over those entrusted to you', and Acts 20:28-29 gives the same charge. The chapter also warns that office can feed the one who holds it. That applies wherever people lead others, in churches, families and organisations.

For ordinary members, the picture of the sheep who trample the pasture is a prescriptive warning too. Strength and comfort are meant to be used for the weaker members, Romans 15:1 and Galatians 6:2, not at their expense.

debates.question: Who is 'My servant David' in verses 23 and 24?

views.label: A coming king from David's line, fulfilled in Christ
views.case: David was long dead, so the promise names a successor. The title 'prince' in verse 24 and the 'one shepherd' of verse 23 agree with Ezekiel 37:24-25, where the servant David is king forever. The New Testament identifies Jesus as the son of David and the good shepherd, Matthew 1:1 and John 10:11. This is the view of the church from the earliest centuries.

views.label: A restored Davidic kingship in the post-exilic community
views.case: Some read the promise as pointing to a Davidic ruler like Zerubbabel, who led the first return, Haggai 2:23. They stress that the first hearers would have expected a person in their own time, and that Ezekiel does not name the Messiah in later categories.

views.label: David himself raised or a personal rule of God
views.case: A smaller number read it as a promise that David will literally return, or take the 'one shepherd' as God Himself, with 'David' as a title for the divine rule. The text distinguishes the two, however: 'I, the LORD, will be their God, and My servant David will be a prince among them', verse 24.

debates.bearing: The text keeps the LORD as shepherd and David as the shepherd He appoints, which looks forward to a person who can be both the LORD's servant and the LORD's own presence with the flock. The New Testament finds that person in Jesus, who is both the Son of David and the one who says, 'I am the good shepherd.'

debates.question: Who are the fat and lean sheep, and the rams and goats, in verses 17 to 22?

views.label: Rich and poor inside Israel
views.case: The charge is that the strong trample the pasture and muddy the water, so the weak feed on what is left. That fits a social setting, where those who had gained wealth in the land pushed aside the weak, a charge made elsewhere by Isaiah and Amos.

views.label: Leaders and followers, or true and false members of the flock
views.case: Some read the 'rams and goats' as a further class of leaders, since the Hebrew words can describe lead animals, and see a continuation of the attack on the shepherds. Others see the sorting of true from false members, which leads naturally to Matthew 25:32-33, where the shepherd separates sheep from goats.

views.label: Israel and the nations
views.case: Less often, the pushing and scattering is applied to the pressure of the nations on the Israelites. The text does not say so, because the sheep who judge and are judged are all 'My flock', verse 17.

debates.bearing: Every reading keeps the point that God cares about the way members of His own people treat each other. The judgment He promises is against the powerful who harm the weak, and the safeguard of the flock is the one shepherd of verse 23.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the oracle is a woe, hoy, the cry of mourning that prophets use to announce a coming judgment, and it falls on the 'shepherds'. The verb behind that noun, ra'ah, means both to shepherd and to feed, which is why the question 'Should not the shepherds feed their flock?' in verse 2 asks at once what a shepherd is and what a shepherd does. The word is widely used of kings, 2 Samuel 5:2, and of God Himself, Psalm 23:1 and Isaiah 40:11, so Ezekiel's accusation is that the human shepherds have abandoned the role that belongs to God.

The five failings of verse 4 are a catalogue of care. 'Strengthened' and 'healed' are the verbs for making strong and for mending, and 'brought back' and 'searched' are verbs of retrieval. The last charge, 'you have ruled them with violence and cruelty', uses the word for harshness that Exodus 1:13 describes with 'ruthlessly', the way Egypt treated the Israelite slaves. The shepherds of Israel have become Pharaohs.

In verse 11 the promise begins, 'I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out'. The first verb, darash, is the one the shepherds were charged with neglecting in verse 6, 'no one to search for them or seek them out', and the second is a close synonym, so the promise answers the charge almost word for word. The phrase 'on a day of clouds and darkness' in verse 12 borrows the language of the day of the LORD, Joel 2:2 and Zephaniah 1:15. The scattering is a kind of judgment, and the rescue is an act within it.

The chapter shifts at verses 23 and 24 from 'shepherd' to 'servant' and 'prince'. 'My servant David' (avdi David) is a title of honour that God gives to David also in 2 Samuel 7:5 and Psalm 89:3. The word for 'prince' (nasi) differs from the word for 'king', and Ezekiel uses it for the ruler of the restored people throughout chapters 40 to 48, so a ruler who stays beneath God and does not claim the throne for himself. In 37:24 the same figure is called 'king'.

The 'covenant of peace' (berit shalom) of verse 25 is an expression of safety and wholeness, the one given to Phinehas in Numbers 25:12 and described as unbreakable in Isaiah 54:10. Ezekiel 37:26 makes it 'an everlasting covenant'. Its content in verses 25 to 29 is a reversal of the covenant curses: wild animals removed, rain in season, the bars of the yoke broken, a land that is secure. The phrase 'showers of blessing' in verse 26 recalls the rains in season of Leviticus 26:4, and 'broken the bars of their yoke' in verse 27 takes up Leviticus 26:13.

Finally, 'a garden of renown' in verse 29 is a phrase whose exact sense is debated. It points to a planting or a place whose fame spreads, and many take it as a land restored to the fruitfulness of a garden, in line with 36:35 and Isaiah 51:3.

typology.fulfillment: David's rise from the sheepfold to the throne, 2 Samuel 7:8 and Psalm 78:70-72, made shepherding the pattern of kingship. Ezekiel promises another David, one who 'will feed them and be their shepherd', verse 23. Jesus is born in David's city and takes the shepherd title as His own, Luke 2:4 and John 10:11, and He is greater than David, since David himself called him Lord, Matthew 22:43-45. David protected the flock from a lion and a bear, 1 Samuel 17:34-35, but he died and could not shepherd forever. Christ lays down His life and takes it up again, John 10:17-18.

The covenant of peace God gave to Phinehas, Numbers 25:12, and promises here as an everlasting bond, is a pattern of security under God's own commitment. It is secured in Christ, 'that great Shepherd of the sheep' who rose 'through the blood of the eternal covenant', Hebrews 13:20. The wild animals that are driven out of the land point to a peace that reaches the creation, Isaiah 11:6-9 and Romans 8:19-21. The type is limited by its place, since a peaceful valley in the land of Israel is a sign, and the fullness is the new creation where nothing harmful remains, Revelation 21:4.

typology.type: The shepherd who seeks the lost
typology.fulfillment: The promise 'I will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken' becomes the parable of the lost sheep, Luke 15:4-7, and the summary of Jesus's mission, 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost', Luke 19:10. Here the type is not a person or event but an action of God, repeated by the Son. The correspondence rises when we see the cost: the shepherd of Ezekiel gathers by power, and the shepherd of John 10 gathers by laying down His life. Zechariah 13:7 and Isaiah 53:6 show the shepherd struck and the sheep's iniquity laid on Him.

God's judgment 'between one sheep and another' in verses 17 to 22 prepares for the great separation in Matthew 25:31-46, where the Son of Man sorts sheep from goats on the ground of how people treated the least of His brothers. The Ezekiel sorting rests on the same ground, how the strong treated the weak, verses 18 to 21. The type reaches its limit in that Ezekiel's sheep and goats are both part of one flock in the present, while Matthew's judgment is final.

typology.type: The flock fed on the mountains of Israel
typology.fulfillment: Rich pasture on the mountains, ravines and settlements of Israel, verses 13 and 14, gives a picture of provision that the New Testament carries into Christ's promise that His sheep will 'find pasture', John 10:9, and of the water the Lamb leads them to, Revelation 7:17. The land is a place and also a sign. Peter's feeding charge to the restored apostle, 'Feed My sheep', John 21:15-17, shows that the Lord's own pasture is provided through those He sends.

study.christ:
Christ is the answer to this chapter at every point of its structure. The shepherds' failure is the failure of every human attempt to care for God's people on their own strength, and the promise is that God Himself comes. When Jesus says 'I am the good shepherd' in John 10:11, He is not borrowing a pleasant image. He is stepping into the place Ezekiel 34 reserves for the LORD and for the one servant David together. The contrast He draws with the hired hand in John 10:12-13, who sees the wolf and runs, is almost a summary of Ezekiel 34:2 to 6.

The chapter leads to Christ by what He does as well as by what He says. 'I Myself will search for My flock' is acted out in the parables of the lost sheep and in the whole journey of the incarnation. The shepherd goes after the sheep, Luke 15:4, and does not wait for it to find its own way home. 'The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost', Luke 19:10, is Ezekiel 34:16 spoken by the one who fulfils it.

There is a twofold identity in Ezekiel that the New Testament joins together. In verse 15 the LORD says 'I will tend My flock', and in verse 23 He appoints 'one shepherd, My servant David'. The tension between God as shepherd and the servant as shepherd is not a contradiction, because in Christ the Lord comes as the Son of David. He is both the LORD who seeks and the servant who feeds, and the one flock 'under one shepherd' of John 10:16 is the fulfilment of verse 23.

The chapter also leads to the cross by a path the prophecy did not itself state. Here the shepherd rescues his sheep from the wild beasts. Jesus says the good shepherd 'lays down His life for the sheep', John 10:11, and the New Testament applies Zechariah 13:7, 'Strike the Shepherd', to His arrest, Matthew 26:31. The covenant of peace of verse 25 is established by His blood, Hebrews 13:20. The language of verse 16, 'bind up the broken', is realised in the one who was wounded for our transgressions, Isaiah 53:5, and Peter ends by saying that the sheep who were going astray have returned 'to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls', 1 Peter 2:25.

Finally, He is the model for all who shepherd under Him. Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves Him, and each time tells him to feed or shepherd His sheep, John 21:15-17. 1 Peter 5:4 calls Christ the Chief Shepherd. The standard of Ezekiel 34:4 is therefore the standard against which every minister is measured, and the grace of verse 11 is the reason any of them can hope to meet it. A caution applies: the chapter itself does not mention the cross, and the links above rest on how the New Testament itself reads Ezekiel 34, not on a hidden meaning.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who owns the flock. Over and over He says 'My flock', 'My shepherds', 'My servant', 'My hill'. The sheep are His before they are anyone's charge, which is why abuse of them is an offence against Him and not merely against them. The shepherds' crime is not that they were poor managers but that they treated the Lord's possession as their own meat. That is why the verdict in verse 10 begins 'Behold, I am against the shepherds', and why He says He will demand His flock from their hand.

He is also a God who moves toward the lost. The 'I will' sentences from verse 11 to verse 16 are among the most active in the Old Testament: search, seek, rescue, bring out, gather, feed, tend, make lie down, seek the lost, bring back, bind up, strengthen. This is not a distant sovereign issuing decrees but a shepherd walking the hills in the dark. Isaiah 40:11 gives the same picture, with the lambs gathered in His arms.

The chapter holds justice and tenderness together without strain. The God who is 'against' the shepherds is the same who 'will shepherd them with justice', verse 16. Care and judgment are two faces of one commitment to the flock. The sorting of verses 17 to 22 shows He is not partial to the powerful among His own people, and that He will not tolerate the strong trampling the weak even within the covenant community.

He keeps His word beyond the failure of human instruments. The monarchy had collapsed, and the leaders had destroyed what they were meant to guard, yet the covenant of peace of verse 25 does not depend on them. It rests on 'I, the LORD, have spoken'. The belonging that ends the chapter, 'You are My flock, the sheep of My pasture, My people, and I am your God', verse 31, comes from His own side. The people did nothing to earn it.

For worship the chapter shapes how we pray and how we serve. We can come to Him as the shepherd who is looking for us, and trust Him with the weak and wandering. Those who lead in His name hold their roles with fear, since the sheep are His. And we give thanks that the covenant of peace is an everlasting one, so that the security of the flock rests on the Shepherd, not on the strength of the sheep.

crossReferences.note: A parallel oracle from the same years. The LORD pronounces woe on shepherds who destroy and scatter His sheep, promises to gather the remnant, and sets over them shepherds who will care for them. Ezekiel 34 goes further in saying that God Himself will do the shepherding, and Jeremiah's next verses, 23:5-6, add the righteous Branch from David.

The best known picture of the LORD as shepherd, with green pastures, still waters and a rod and staff in the valley. Ezekiel 34:13-15 draws on it, with its promises that He will feed them in good pasture and make them lie down. The psalm is in the first person, 'I shall not want', and Ezekiel gives the same security to a whole scattered nation.

The covenant with David that stands behind 'My servant David'. God took him from the pasture and promised a house and a throne that would last forever. Ezekiel's shepherd is the heir of that promise, and the phrase 'My servant' is the same title God uses of David in 7:5 and 7:8.

The covenant blessings that Ezekiel 34:25-27 deliberately echoes: rain in season, the land yielding its produce, dangerous animals removed, and the bars of the yoke broken. The promise of the restored flock is a return to blessings that Israel had lost by breaking the covenant, and God Himself now secures them.

Zechariah acts out the role of a shepherd of a doomed flock, and the passage ends with a worthless shepherd who deserts the sheep and devours the choice ones. It carries Ezekiel's accusation forward and shows that the problem of bad shepherds remained after the exile, so that the promise in Ezekiel 34 still waited.

Jesus sees the crowds, harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, and is moved with compassion. The words are a quiet allusion to Ezekiel 34:5 and Numbers 27:17, and they show that the condition the prophet described was still true in His own day. His response is to heal and teach, and to send out workers.

The parable of the lost sheep puts Ezekiel 34:11 and 16 into the mouth of Jesus. A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find one that is lost, and he carries it home with joy. The parable answers the grumbling of the Pharisees, who looked more like Ezekiel's shepherds than like the God they claimed to serve.

The great shepherd discourse. Jesus calls Himself the good shepherd, contrasts Himself with hired hands and thieves, speaks of laying down His life, and promises 'one flock and one shepherd'. Ezekiel 34 is the main background, and the claim to be the shepherd who gathers and the one who lays down his life gives the old promise its cost.

Peter charges elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain and not by lording it over them, and promises a crown when the Chief Shepherd appears. It is Ezekiel 34:2 to 4 turned into pastoral instruction, and it shows the standard has not changed. The Chief Shepherd stands behind every undershepherd.

The benediction names Jesus as the great Shepherd of the sheep, raised from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant. It joins the shepherd of Ezekiel 34:23 to the everlasting covenant of 37:26, and says that the covenant of peace is ratified by His blood.

The multitude before the throne is shepherded by the Lamb, who leads them to springs of living water and wipes away every tear. It is the end of the long promise: the flock safe, fed and watered, no longer prey, under a shepherd who is also the sacrificed Lamb.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a gardener, a man who is told to work the garden and keep it, Genesis 2:15, and it quickly turns into the story of a world that needs a shepherd. Abel is a keeper of flocks, Genesis 4:2. The patriarchs are shepherds, Moses leads the sheep of Jethro before he leads the flock of Israel out of Egypt, and David the shepherd boy is made king. Through all of it the quiet question stands: who will care for God's people? Israel's kings were meant to answer it, and chapter 34 is the verdict on how they did. The earlier chapters of the book have already said that the shepherds were guilty, and this chapter says what God will do about it.

It is the point in the story where God moves from judging the failed institutions to promising to do the work Himself. The same God who scattered the flock in judgment will gather it. That is the pivot between the ruin of chapter 33 and the great promises of chapters 36 and 37, with the new heart, the dry bones raised and the one king over a united people. The 'one shepherd' of 34:23 returns as 'one king' and 'one shepherd for all of them' in 37:24, and the covenant of peace of 34:25 becomes the everlasting covenant of 37:26.

The promise is taken up by the Gospels with remarkable directness. Jesus sees crowds without a shepherd, tells of the lost sheep, and names Himself the good shepherd. The cross shows what the shepherd's care costs, and the resurrection gives Him as the great Shepherd of the sheep, Hebrews 13:20. The church is the flock He gathers from every nation, John 10:16, and its elders serve under the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4.

The ending of the story is the end of chapter 34 fully realised. In the new creation 'the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd', Revelation 7:17, there is no hunger or thirst and no scorching heat, and the dangerous beasts of Ezekiel's day have no place. The God who said 'You are My flock... and I am your God' hears it said back by a multitude no one can count, and 'God Himself will be with them as their God', Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: The Shepherd-King
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly from Ezekiel 34:11-17 and 23-29, tracing the LORD's promise to shepherd His scattered flock Himself and to appoint His servant David as the one shepherd, exactly the movement from failed human shepherds to Christ the Good Shepherd this study is built around.

quiz.q: What is the specific charge against Israel's shepherds in verses 2-4?

options.text: They fed themselves, not the flock, neglecting the weak, sick, injured, strayed, and lost, and ruled with force and cruelty.
options.note: Verses 3-4 list this exact set of failures in detail.

options.text: They failed to build enough sheepfolds for the winter.
options.note: No mention of sheepfolds appears; the charge concerns neglect and self-serving cruelty, not infrastructure.

options.text: They demanded excessive tax payments from the flock.
options.note: The imagery is pastoral, not fiscal; the charge is about neglect and abuse of care, not taxation.

options.text: They abandoned the flock entirely and left the country.
options.note: They did not leave; they stayed and fed off the flock while failing to care for it, verses 3-4.

quiz.q: What does God Himself promise to do because of the shepherds' failure, verses 11-12 and 15-16?

options.text: Search for His scattered flock Himself, rescue them, and shepherd them, seeking the lost and binding up the injured.
options.note: Verses 11-12, 15-16 state this promise directly and repeatedly.

options.text: Appoint a committee of new human shepherds to replace the old ones immediately.
options.note: God promises to act Himself first, verse 11, before the later appointment of one shepherd in verse 23.

options.text: Destroy the whole flock and begin again with a new one.
options.note: The opposite is promised: rescue, gathering, and tender care for the existing flock.

options.text: Leave the flock scattered as a permanent judgment on their leaders' sin.
options.note: God explicitly reverses the scattering rather than leaving it permanent, verses 12-13.

quiz.q: What judgment does God pronounce between the sheep themselves in verses 17-22?

options.text: He will judge between the fat and lean sheep, holding accountable those who trampled pasture and muddied water needed by the weak.
options.note: Verses 18-20 describe exactly this trampling, muddying, and God's resulting judgment.

options.text: He will judge only the shepherds and never examine the sheep themselves.
options.note: Verses 17 and 20 explicitly extend judgment to the sheep, not only the shepherds.

options.text: He will reward the fattest, strongest sheep as the most faithful.
options.note: The opposite occurs: the strong who abuse the weak are judged and the weak are rescued, verses 16, 20-22.

options.text: No distinctions are made among the sheep at all.
options.note: Clear distinctions are made between fat and lean, rams and goats, verses 17, 20.

quiz.q: Who does God appoint as the one shepherd over His flock in verses 23-24?

options.text: His servant David, who will feed them and be their shepherd while the LORD is their God.
options.note: Verses 23-24 name 'My servant David' directly as the appointed shepherd and prince.

options.text: A newly chosen priest from the line of Levi.
options.note: The appointed figure is specifically called 'My servant David,' not a Levitical priest.

options.text: Ezekiel himself, appointed directly as Israel's shepherd.
options.note: Ezekiel is the messenger of this promise, not its subject; the appointed shepherd is 'My servant David.'

options.text: No shepherd is appointed; God rules the flock without any mediator.
options.note: A specific shepherd, David, is explicitly appointed, even while the LORD remains their God, verses 23-24.

quiz.q: What does the covenant of peace in verses 25-29 include?

options.text: Security from wild beasts, showers of blessing, fruitful land, and freedom from famine and the nations' scorn.
options.note: Verses 25-29 list each of these specific covenant blessings in turn.

options.text: Only a temporary ceasefire with surrounding nations.
options.note: The covenant is described as far more comprehensive than a political truce, covering safety, provision, and blessing.

options.text: The abolition of agriculture in favor of direct, miraculous provision.
options.note: The covenant promises fruitful trees and yielding land, verse 27, not the end of agriculture.

options.text: Nothing specific; the covenant's contents are left entirely undefined.
options.note: The covenant's contents are spelled out in specific detail across verses 25-29.

questions: Israel's shepherds fed themselves at the flock's expense. Where might you be using a position of care, leadership, or trust for your own benefit rather than for those God has placed under you?
God says, 'I Myself will search for My flock and seek them out.' How does knowing God personally, actively searches for the lost and wandering change how you view your own wandering seasons?
God judges between the fat sheep who trampled the pasture and the lean sheep left with only muddied water. Where might your comfort or plenty be coming at the expense of someone weaker near you?

Jesus claims this chapter's promise directly: 'I am the good shepherd; the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.' What would it look like, practically this week, to trust that He is actively shepherding you rather than leaving you to fend for yourself?
The covenant of peace promises security, provision, and freedom from fear. Where in your life do you most need to trust the Shepherd's covenant rather than your own vigilance?

translationNotes.note: 'My servant David' does not mean the historical King David returning to life; it is a prophetic title identifying the coming Messiah as David's promised heir, since the ministry and reign described here is everlasting.

'Covenant of peace' (berit shalom) names a single, comprehensive covenant of well-being, echoed again in Ezekiel 37:26 and Numbers 25:12, bundling security, provision, and right relationship with God into one promise.

Some translations render part of verse 31 as 'human sheep,' reflecting an unusual construction in the underlying Hebrew that simply emphasizes these are God's own people, His flock in the fullest covenantal sense, not merely animals under a shepherd.
